title: Planted run file in the runs folder makes cra status report a healthy latest run
description: A run record placed in the `--runs` folder with a newer `finished_at` and self-declared healthy fields replaces the genuine latest run in `cra status`. The status output then reads "Latest run: all sources ok." and exits 0, hiding a genuine REPORT CASE finding that the real run recorded.
impact: The `status` command is the operator's only safety signal between scheduled `cra run` calls. With write access to the runs folder, a single file hides an earlier REPORT CASE warning and makes status exit 0 with a fresh "last successful run" time. The integrity of the status verdict depends entirely on the folder contents. Confidentiality and availability are not affected. Integrity impact is limited to the operator-visible status verdict.
target: cra CLI (local, src/news_watcher.py status_summary / run_is_complete / load_runs)
technical_analysis:
`status_summary` takes the latest run as `runs[-1]` after `load_runs` sorts every `*.json` file in the runs folder by its own `finished_at` value. It then decides health from fields the file itself declares: `run_is_complete` checks only `complete is True` and that every entry in `sources` has `status == "ok"` (`src/news_watcher.py:585-594`). The other health checks (`report_cases`, `needs_human`, `components.unchecked`, `result.data_gaps`, `sbom_warnings`) are also read straight from the same file. Nothing in the code binds a run record to the process that wrote it. There is no digest, no sequence number, and no cross-check against the genuine run history.

def load_runs(run_dir):
    runs = []
    paths = sorted(Path(run_dir).glob("*.json"))[-MAX_RUN_FILES:]
    for path in paths:
        data = _read_json(path)
        if isinstance(data, dict) and isinstance(data.get("finished_at"), str):
            runs.append((_parse_time(data["finished_at"]), path.stem, data))
    ...
```

        lines.append("Latest run: all sources ok.")
```

The only protection against a future-dated planted run is `last_time <= current`. A planted file dated slightly before "now" passes it. The project records this as an accepted residual risk (PROGRESS.md, "Cache and run files can be edited by anyone with write access to the project folder", and PLAN.md section (b)). This report keeps the finding visible because the README warning and status wording are the only mitigation, and status presents the result as a verdict.

4. Run `python -m src status --runs <folder>` again. The output reads "Latest run: all sources ok." with no REPORT CASE warning, and the exit code is 0.

remediation_steps: Treat the status verdict as only as trustworthy as the runs folder, and make that explicit. Two options for the project owner to decide. (a) Add an integrity seal to each run record at save time (a digest of its canonical content, verified in `load_runs`, with unsealed or mismatched files treated as unreadable and surfaced as a warning). This stops accidental and naive edits, not a determined local writer, and needs a decision on key handling. (b) Keep the current design but have `status` print a visible warning when the newest run file is not the newest file written by the tool, and document the limit in the README. Whichever option is chosen, make sure a file that cannot be verified never produces "Latest run: all sources ok.".

The exit code changes from 1 to 0. The genuine record that says `report_cases: 2` is still present in the folder but is no longer consulted. Reproduced at `/workspace/poc-output/poc/poc_planted_run_status.py` in the copy.
assumptions: Attacker has write access to the `--runs` folder (same account or a shared folder). Attacker knows the record format, which is public in the source. No network access is needed.
counterevidence: 1. The project explicitly accepts this. PLAN.md section (b) and PROGRESS.md ("Cache and run files can be edited by anyone with write access to the project folder ... accepted") say that fingerprints would only guard against mistakes, and the README is to say so. This report therefore reports a known, accepted limitation, not an unknown bug. 2. The attacker needs local write access to the project folder. The same access already allows editing `evidence/` and the cache, so this is not a privilege gain. The attacker is not the SBOM supplier in the threat model. 3. Future-dated files are rejected (`last_time <= current` and the "dated in the future" warning), so the attacker must date the file within the window. This does not stop the attack, but it constrains it. 4. The genuine run record is not deleted, so a human who reads the folder can still see it. 5. The status command still prints the "26-hour" and reporting-deadline notes. None of these stop a file that declares healthy fields from being trusted. The check that ran was: does the latest record's own flags say complete, and it does.
severity_change_conditions: Raise to Medium if the runs folder can be written by a different principal than the operator (a shared network folder, a scheduler account, or a sync tool), or if an automated consumer (alerting, dashboard, Power BI from PLAN.md phase 5) treats `status` exit 0 as an all-clear. title: cra status loads every planted run file into memory without a total size budget
description: `cra status` reads up to 1000 `*.json` files from the runs folder, each up to 20 MB, and keeps every parsed record in memory, although only the newest and the newest healthy record are used. A folder holding many large files can exhaust memory and make `status` fail.
impact: Denial of service of the `status` command. A local writer to the runs folder can make `status` consume several gigabytes of memory, slow it down, or crash it with a MemoryError. The operator then cannot check the last run. Data is not disclosed and not modified.
technical_analysis:
`load_runs` selects the newest `MAX_RUN_FILES` (1000) paths by name, and for each one calls `_read_json`, which reads up to `MAX_CACHE_FILE_BYTES` (20 MB) and parses the JSON. Every parsed record that has a string `finished_at` is appended to `runs` and kept until the function returns. `status_summary` then uses only `runs[-1]` and the newest record that passes `run_is_complete`. Per-file size is capped, but the total is not, so memory grows with the file count times the per-file cap.

```python title=news_watcher.py startLineNumber=601 endLineNumber=612 
def load_runs(run_dir):
    runs = []
    paths = sorted(Path(run_dir).glob("*.json"))[-MAX_RUN_FILES:]
    for path in paths:
        data = _read_json(path)
        if isinstance(data, dict) and isinstance(data.get("finished_at"), str):
            runs.append((_parse_time(data["finished_at"]), path.stem, data))
    ...
```

def _read_json(path):
    try:
        ...
        with open(path, "rb") as handle:
            raw = handle.read(MAX_CACHE_FILE_BYTES + 1)

Keep only the newest run and the newest run that passes the completeness check while reading, instead of retaining every record. Add a total byte budget for the run folder. Make a skipped or oversized file visible: if the budget or the count cap drops a newer file, `status` must print a warning and must not report "Latest run: all sources ok.", so that a dropped run cannot hide behind an older healthy run. The project owner should decide the budget size and the wording of that warning.

The run still exited normally, because the padded files lack the fields needed for a real run record. The per-record cost is therefore about 20 MB of RAM and about 0.07 s of CPU per file. The check that ran was: does the loader bound the total bytes it reads or keeps? It does not.
confidence_rationale: Memory use per file was measured (821 MB for 40 files). The 1000-file worst case is extrapolated and was not run, so the stated ceiling is unconfirmed. The exact point of failure depends on the host.
severity_change_conditions: Raise to Medium if an automated job runs `cra status` on a shared or network folder that other principals can write to, so that a remote writer can crash the scheduler's health check. title: Slash-separated or upper-case Maven purl is accepted as OK and silently clears an exploited component
description: A CycloneDX component whose Maven purl uses a slash-separated namespace, such as `pkg:maven/org/apache/logging/log4j/log4j-core@2.14.1`, or an upper-case group or artifact spelling, is accepted as a valid component. OSV does not match these spellings, so `cra run` reports the component as checked with zero findings, a complete result, and exit code 0. The canonical form of the same component is affected by CVE-2021-44228, which is listed in CISA KEV.
impact: A supplier-supplied or hand-edited SBOM can make the tool report a vulnerable Maven component as clean. The run record is marked complete, the console prints `No exploited vulnerabilities found in the checked components (all sources ok)`, and `cra status` reports `Latest run: all sources ok.` A KEV-listed affected component is therefore never raised for the 24-hour early-warning decision. The same silence applies to every advisory for that component, not only the exploited one.
technical_analysis: The SBOM reader validates each component purl and then rebuilds a canonical purl from its parts. For Maven, the namespace is split on the slash character and every segment is accepted independently, so org/apache/logging/log4j passes as a namespace (sbom_reader.py lines 146 to 149). The group-field check only compares the purl namespace with its dotted form, so a matching group field also passes. The name and group checks use exact comparison, so upper-case spellings pass too. The canonical purl is then sent to OSV unchanged. OSV querybatch is case-sensitive and does not normalize slashes, so it returns no advisories for these spellings. In matcher.evaluate the component therefore has an empty advisory list, produces no finding, and is counted in checked. match_vulnerability only returns UNKNOWN when OSV listed the vulnerability for that purl, so nothing downstream notices the mismatch. feeds.complete is then true, so the run record and cra status both report success. An existing test, test_double_slash_in_a_namespace_is_cleaned_up_not_kept, pins the acceptance of the slash form as OK. Measured against live OSV on the same component: the canonical purl returns 7 advisories, including GHSA-jfh8-c2jp-5v3q (CVE-2021-44228, KEV-listed). The slash-namespace, upper-case group, and upper-case artifact variants each return 0 advisories. Root cause: the reader accepts non-canonical identifiers as equivalent to the canonical component without checking that they are spelled the way the vulnerability database spells them, and an absent advisory answer is treated as a clean result.

Run check-sbom on the SBOM; the component is listed as OK. 4. Repeat with pkg:maven/ORG.apache.logging.log4j/log4j-core@2.14.1 (upper-case group); the result matches step 4.

Update the test that currently expects the slash form to be OK so that it expects UNKNOWN, and add regression tests for both forms. This converts the silent clean result for these spellings into UNKNOWN and RESULT INCOMPLETE for human review.

Canonical namespace, same component and same feeds: `[REPORT CASE (affected AND actively exploited - the 24-hour clock may be running)] log4j-core 2.14.1: GHSA-jfh8-c2jp-5v3q (CVE-2021-44228) -> AFFECTED [osv_exact_version_list] - ACTIVELY EXPLOITED per kev (CVE-2021-44228)` and exit code 3. Live OSV querybatch for pkg:maven/org.apache.logging.log4j/log4j-core@2.14.1 returns 7 advisories; the same query with pkg:maven/org/apache/logging/log4j/log4j-core@2.14.1, pkg:maven/ORG.apache.logging.log4j/log4j-core@2.14.1 and pkg:maven/org.apache.logging.log4j/Log4j-Core@2.14.1 returns an empty result each. counterevidence: Checked: mainstream generators (CycloneDX Maven plugin, Syft) emit dot-separated canonical namespaces, so the trigger needs a hand-written, edited, or defective SBOM. This lowers likelihood but not the validity of the defect. Checked whether check-sbom or run surfaces anything: check-sbom prints OK and run prints only Components checked: 1, so the operator is not warned. Checked whether the matcher's osv_listed safety rule catches it: it does not, because OSV returned nothing to compare. Checked whether the run is marked incomplete: it is marked complete. No control in the reader, matcher, or CLI prevents the silent clear for these spellings.

If the SBOM were ingested automatically from a network channel without operator action, the rating would rise to High (7.5); cross-checking component identity against a second source would lower it to Low.

title: Same-version range boundaries misordered, hiding reintroduced affected versions
description: The OSV range walk in the CRA matcher sorts a fixed boundary before a later introduced boundary at the same version. A version that is affected again after the reintroduction is therefore computed as not affected. The evaluation step then reports it as UNKNOWN, so an actively exploited (KEV-listed) affected component gets urgent human review instead of a report case.
impact: A component affected by a KEV-listed vulnerability through a same-version reintroduction is routed to URGENT_HUMAN_REVIEW instead of REPORT_CASE. The matcher's direct result for the same version is NOT_AFFECTED. Demonstrated with a crafted OSV-style record; the scope is limited to range shapes with a same-version end and start inside one range.
technical_analysis: _intervals converts OSV introduced, fixed and last_affected events into start, end and inclusive spans. It sorts the parsed events by (version, is_end), so at an equal version every start is placed before every end. The loop then skips a start while a span is already open. For a range introduced 2.0-beta9, fixed 2.12.2, introduced 2.12.2, the sorted order is introduced 2.0-beta9, introduced 2.12.2, fixed 2.12.2. The second start is skipped as redundant, and the fixed event closes the span at 2.12.2. The span that the event list describes as open from 2.12.2 onward is lost, so the version 2.14.1 falls outside every span and match_vulnerability returns NOT_AFFECTED (maven_numeric_range). Only the written order distinguishes this case from a zero-width span, so ties must keep the order in which the events were written. evaluate passes osv_listed=True, so the matcher's NOT_AFFECTED is converted to UNKNOWN (osv_says_affected_but_our_check_disagrees). For a KEV-listed CVE this yields URGENT_HUMAN_REVIEW rather than REPORT_CASE.

3. Check pkg:maven/org.apache.logging.log4j/log4j-core@2.14.1. The reintroduction at 2.12.2 is open-ended, so 2.14.1 is affected; the correct answer is AFFECTED.
4. Evaluate the same component with a KEV list containing CVE-2021-44228. The correct action is REPORT_CASE.

title: Substituted CISA KEV list is accepted as complete, silently dropping exploited CVEs
description: The KEV completeness check in `cra run` accepts any structurally valid KEV list whose count does not fall more than 5% below the highest count seen before. A network attacker who can intercept the CISA KEV download can remove two known-exploited entries and the tool still reports the KEV source as `ok` and the run as complete. A product whose affected component is actively exploited is then downgraded from REPORT CASE to RECORD.
impact: An on-path attacker who can serve a modified CISA KEV response can (a) remove specific known-exploited CVEs so that affected components are reported as not exploited, turning a REPORT CASE (the 24-hour early-warning clock) into a RECORD, while the run record and `cra status` show "all sources ok" and `complete: true`; and (b) replay the previous KEV list with an advanced `dateReleased`, so CVEs added in the genuine update are absent from the run for the intercepted run. The tool gives no warning for either case.
target: cra-scan CLI, KEV download (www.cisa.gov known_exploited_vulnerabilities.json), src/news_watcher.py
technical_analysis:
The KEV download is validated in `validate_kev` and stored by `fetch_kev`. The only protection against a shortened list is a count tolerance:

```python title=src/news_watcher.py startLineNumber=224 endLineNumber=225
    if saved_max_count and len(entries) < saved_max_count * (1 - MAX_KEV_DROP):
        return "KEV count dropped by more than 5% compared with the highest count seen before"
```

`MAX_KEV_DROP` is `0.05` (`src/news_watcher.py:46`). The check only compares cardinality, so removing any number of entries up to 5% of the list is accepted, and removing entries while adding the same number of invented CVE ids (which pass the CVE pattern, uniqueness and date checks) is also accepted. The download is then stored as a good copy in `fetch_kev` (`src/news_watcher.py:253-254`, `_write_json_atomic` at the end of `fetch_kev`), `status` is set to `ok`, and `Feeds.sources_ok`/`complete` report the run complete. Nothing in the matcher cross-checks the KEV list against the previous copy; `exploited_status` only tests membership in `kev_ids`.

The removal in the proof of concept targets the two KEV entries that are the only KEV links for the affected log4j-core 2.14.1 records (CVE-2021-44228 and CVE-2021-45046). Removing both is 0.11% of the list, far below the 5% tolerance. The 5% tolerance is explicitly tested as intended behaviour (`tests/test_news_watcher.py`, "drop of less than 5 percent is accepted"), so the design choice itself is the root of the completeness gap: the tool asserts completeness and freshness from structure alone.

Replay variant: `validate_kev` only rejects a `dateReleased` older than the saved copy. An on-path response that carries the previous entries with a newer `dateReleased` passes, is saved, and is reported `ok`. A later uninterrupted run then recovers the new entries, so the effect lasts for the intercepted run(s).

The first run has no saved copy and no baseline, so any list of 1000 or more entries is accepted as complete on the first download. This is a related residual and is not separately demonstrated here.

Git history is not available in the checked-out source, so no commit attribution is given.

Every later genuine KEV download is then rejected as "older than the saved copy (possible replay)", so the tool keeps using the frozen copy and no longer picks up new KEV entries until the operator deletes the cache file.

title: Total download deadline is not enforced during reads, so a slow response can stall a run indefinitely
description: `http_fetch` applies a 120-second total deadline, but checks it only between `read()` calls. `HTTPResponse.read(64 * 1024)` blocks until 64 KB arrive or the connection closes, so a server that sends a byte every few seconds keeps one read open and defeats the deadline. The per-read socket timeout only catches silence longer than 30 seconds, so a drip below that interval stalls `cra run` for as long as the server keeps dribbling bytes.
impact: An on-path attacker who can serve OSV or KEV responses can make a single download take an unbounded time, which stops the scheduled `cra run` from finishing. No run record is written for the stalled run, so the last saved record ages until `cra status` reports the run as overdue. The check is interrupted only when the operator kills the process.
target: cra-scan CLI, OSV and KEV downloads, src/news_watcher.py (http_fetch)
technical_analysis:
The deadline and the read loop are in `http_fetch`:

```python title=src/news_watcher.py startLineNumber=100 endLineNumber=111
        with opener.open(request, timeout=TIMEOUT_SECONDS) as response:
            expected = response.headers.get("Content-Length")
            chunks, size = [], 0
            while True:
                if time.monotonic() > deadline:
                    raise FetchError("download took too long")
                chunk = response.read(64 * 1024)
                if not chunk:
                    break
```

`http.client.HTTPResponse.read(amt)` on a close-delimited or Content-Length body keeps reading from the socket until `amt` bytes are available or the stream ends. The loop therefore checks the deadline only after a full 64 KB chunk or end-of-stream. The socket timeout (`TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, 30 s) resets with each received byte, so a server that sends one byte every 25 seconds never triggers it.

Measured with the unmodified code against a local TLS server (`TOTAL_SECONDS` = 120 and `TIMEOUT_SECONDS` = 30 as shipped):
- 8 bytes sent 20 seconds apart: the call returned `download took too long` after 160.0 s, after the server closed the stream, not at the 120 s cap.
- 100000 bytes sent 25 seconds apart: no return within the 200-second hard limit used by the test harness, so the call would continue for about 2.5 million seconds.

The unit test for the deadline (`test_http_fetch_overall_time_limit`) mocks `time.monotonic` and does not exercise the blocking read, so it does not catch this.

    print("returned", len(raw), "bytes after", round(time.monotonic() - start, 1), "s")

title: OSV vulnerability id with a trailing dot aborts the whole run
description: The id pattern used for OSV responses accepts an identifier that ends with a dot, but the file-name check used when the id is turned into a cache path rejects it. A feed response that lists such an id raises an uncaught `ValueError` inside `fetch_osv`, which aborts `cra run` for every component. The run is recorded as an internal error and is not completed.
impact: An on-path attacker who can serve one OSV batch response can stop every `cra run` from completing while that response is served. The tool fails safe (the run is marked incomplete and the operator is told), so no false "nothing found" result is produced; the impact is an availability loss for the scheduled check.
target: cra-scan CLI, OSV batch and detail download, src/news_watcher.py
technical_analysis:
The id is validated by `VULN_ID_PATTERN`, which accepts a trailing dot:

```python title=src/news_watcher.py startLineNumber=56 endLineNumber=56
VULN_ID_PATTERN = re.compile(r"(?!.*\.\.)[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,63}")  # no ".." anywhere
```

The id then reaches `_vuln_cache_path`, which builds the file name `osv-<id>.json` and passes it to `safe_join`. `safe_join` rejects any name that ends with a dot (`src/safe_paths.py`, `name.endswith(".")`), so the same id is refused with a `ValueError`. The call site in `fetch_osv` is outside every `try` block:

```python title=src/news_watcher.py startLineNumber=511 endLineNumber=511
        path = _vuln_cache_path(cache_dir, vuln_id)
```

Only `FetchError` is caught in that loop, so the `ValueError` propagates to `collect` and `_run`. `_run` catches `Exception`, prints `RESULT INCOMPLETE - internal error (ValueError)` and saves a failed run record. The two validators agree on every other id class; the mismatch is limited to the trailing dot. Identifiers with a trailing dot do not occur in OSV data, which is why this is a robustness defect in a feed-controlled input rather than a data-integrity issue.

2. Run `cra run` with an SBOM that contains that component and a valid KEV list.
3. Observe the internal-error abort, the failed run record, and that the other components are not reported.

A record of this failed run was saved; `cra status` will show it.

title: Concurrent run records in the same second overwrite each other
description: `save_run` checks whether the run file name is free and then writes it in a separate step. Two runs that finish in the same UTC second can both see the name as free and both write it, so the later write replaces the earlier run record. In the measured case, 16 concurrent saves left one or two files on disk. A complete run can therefore replace an incomplete one in the same second, and `cra status` then shows the replacement.
impact: Two `cra run` processes that finish in the same second (for example an overlapping scheduled job and a manual run) can lose one run record. If the surviving record is a complete run that replaced an incomplete one, `cra status` reports a complete latest run and hides the failure. The impact is limited to the operator's own run history; no remote party can trigger it.
target: cra-scan CLI, run record folder, src/news_watcher.py (save_run)
technical_analysis:
The name check and the write are separate steps:

```python title=src/news_watcher.py startLineNumber=575 endLineNumber=581
    stamp = now().strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H-%M-%SZ")
    path = run_dir / f"{stamp}.json"
    counter = 1
    while path.exists():
        counter += 1
        path = run_dir / f"{stamp}-{counter:04d}.json"  # zero-padded so the order stays right
    _write_json_atomic(path, run)
```

`_write_json_atomic` finishes with `os.replace`, which overwrites an existing file. Between `path.exists()` returning False and the replace, another process can create the same name. The write is still atomic, so no partial file is seen, but the earlier record is gone. Run names have one-second resolution, so the window is the time between the check and the replace in two processes that finish in the same second.

Measured on the unmodified source: 16 threads calling `save_run` behind a barrier with a fixed time left 1, 1 and 2 run files in three repetitions, from 16 saves. With an exclusive create (`O_EXCL`) claiming the name first, the same test kept 16 of 16 files in every trial. The existing test `test_save_run_does_not_overwrite_a_run_from_the_same_second` covers only sequential saves, which is why it did not catch this.

2. Start 16 threads that each call `save_run` with the same fixed time, released together with a barrier (two overlapping `cra run` processes that finish in the same second produce the same condition).
3. Count the run files afterwards. On the unmodified source the count is far below 16.

import threading
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

runs = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
fixed = datetime(2026, 10, 25, 12, 0, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
barrier = threading.Barrier(16)


def saver(index):
    barrier.wait()
    nw.save_run(runs, {"finished_at": fixed.isoformat(), "writer": index}, lambda: fixed)


threads = [threading.Thread(target=saver, args=(i,)) for i in range(16)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:

print("16 concurrent saves in the same second -> run files on disk:", len(list(runs.glob("*.json"))))

title: Run record above 20 MB is silently skipped by cra status, which then reports the previous clean run as current
description: cra run saves its full result, including every finding, with no size limit, but cra status silently skips any run file over its 20 MB read cap. An SBOM with many duplicate components can push the saved run past that cap, so cra status reports an older complete run as the latest run with exit code 0, even when the skipped run contains a REPORT CASE.
impact: The status command, which is the scheduled health check, can show a false all-clear while the latest run found an affected and actively exploited component. The run command itself still prints the REPORT CASE and exits with code 3, so the loss is limited to the status view and to operators who rely on it. The effect is an incorrect integrity signal for the early-warning check, with no confidentiality or availability impact.

The SBOM controls the size: duplicate component entries each produce a full set of findings for the same advisories. A live run with 1000 identical pypi django 1.0.1 components plus one maven log4j-core 2.14.1 component produced 88007 findings and a 50.5 MB run file. A 14 MB run file from a smaller SBOM (25508 findings) is still read, so the cap is reachable from a small SBOM. This is distinct from the already-filed planted-run-file finding, because the file is written by the tool itself and the defect is the silent skip.

When a run file exists but is too large or unreadable, status must treat it as the latest run and report it as incomplete, using the file modification time as its time. Also keep saved runs within a size the reader accepts, or raise the reader limit to match the writer, so a legitimate run is not dropped.

A 24 MB run file (42515 findings) gives the same false result. A 14 MB run file (25508 findings) in the same folder gives WARNING: the latest run found 2 REPORT CASE finding(s) (affected AND actively exploited). Check the 24-hour deadline. with exit code 1, which shows the size cap is the only difference. With the fix applied in the working copy, the 24 MB file is reported as WARNING: RESULT INCOMPLETE with run_file: failed - the saved run is too large to read and exit code 1.
assumptions: An earlier complete run exists in the same runs folder, and the operator relies on cra status rather than the console output of cra run. The SBOM may come from a third party or be large in the operator's own environment.

severity_change_conditions: If the scheduled job exposes only the status exit code to an alerting system with no other review, the rating rises to Medium; if the run command output is always reviewed, it drops to informational.
